title: Gateless Barrier, Case 8: Hsi-chang Builds Carts
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Case 8 of the Mumonkan, in Nyogen Senzaki's translation, where a teacher asks whether Hsi-chang is still a master wheelmaker if the hub is removed from his fifty-spoke wheels. Nomon removes parts one at a time to find where a wheel stops being a wheel, and ties the question to emptiness, svabhava, and the Metta Sutta's line about the wise holding no fixed views. Old photographs of Nomon at 22 and at 10, and of this room as an empty shell, show how each person sees a different room. Chapter 11 of the Dao De Jing, in Red Pine's translation, praises the empty space in the hub, and Nomon compares it to a shuso, terrified at first to be the hub, who finds the wheel turns itself.

Oh well, continuing to explore these old Zen stories.
Zen is famous for our stories, so I don't know why.
Some of them are great, some of them are a little bit strange.
This is the eighth story in the Mumonkan koan collection.
This time I'm using Nogin Senzaki's translation.
I like that a little better than Robert Aitken's.
*Yu Yan said to his students, "Zishong, the first wheelmaker in China, made two wheels of fifty spokes each.
Now suppose you remove the hub uniting the spokes.
What would become of the wheel?
If Zishong had done this, could he still be called a master wheelmaker?"*
So Yu Yan is a teacher talking about an ancient figure named Zishong.
Here it is again.
*Yu Yan said to his students, "Zishong, the first great wheelmaker in China, the first wheelmaker in China, made two wheels of fifty spokes each.
Now suppose you remove the hub uniting the spokes.
What would become of the wheel?
If Zishong had done this, could he still be called a master wheelmaker?"*
It turns out in Chinese mythology, Chinese stories, Zishong is the one who invented the wheel.
So they know who invented the wheel in China.
I suppose if any culture is going to take credit for inventing the wheel, the Chinese probably can make a pretty good case.
So right away this story is invoking deep history, invoking authority, invoking the ultimate.
Zishong's wheels are the original wheels, the first wheels, the true wheels.
So this represents the nature of wheel, wheel-ness if you will.
So right away we should be wondering, what is this deep question about the true nature of wheels?
The teacher asks his students about the way we think about things, the way we make concepts of things.
What if you took the hub out?
Is it still a wheel?
And if Zishong, this ancient figure, was a master wheelmaker and his wheels don't have hubs, is he still a wheelmaker?
We can all picture this, and I think at this point we would say, no question, well, that's a wheel without a hub.
Sure it's a wheel.
Anybody can see that.
So then what if we took away the spokes?
Or took away the rim?
Then maybe you'd say, oh, that's a rim, or that's a pile of spokes.
Or maybe you aren't quite sure.
It's a pile of sort of straight little wood or metal rods.
Could be anything.
Is that a rim of a wheel or a hoop for a barrel?
Or some kind of art piece?
Some kind of junk?
At some point we don't know it's a wheel anymore.
Of course this is all common sense, so why waste your time on this?
There are probably more important things to talk about.
But it is worth thinking about, I think: the way we make things into things.
This is one of the themes of our teachings on emptiness, which are hard to understand, because the mechanism we have for understanding things is a little bit undercut by emptiness.
We like common sense.
We say, that's common sense, and if it's common sense it must be true.
But these teachings suggest that although common sense is good as far as it goes, it's a helpful kind of shortcut when we try to understand what's happening with us, with each other, with our world.
Wheels are just an example.
Common sense can also blind us.
Common sense can also confuse us.
Common sense can cause us to miss it in fundamental ways.
So the idea is to really notice the way we use concepts.
We do this without thinking about it, or maybe nothing but thinking about it.
We use concepts to define things and separate things and to sort of validate and make sense of our world.
And we use them very quickly.
The brain is very fast.
A hundred, or is it a thousand billion neurons, lots of neurons, working overtime all the time.
I read that when they were first doing real-time brain research, they put people in the brain scanner.
They would be like, why is there all that activity?
We haven't asked the guy to do anything.
So they just ignored that data.
Later they figured out, well, actually there are things happening all the time that matter in the brain.
And this is what's happening.
The brain is conceptualizing, making sense of things, separating things.
The thing about it is that as soon as we separate something, we miss something too.
We stop at a surface.
We stop at an edge.
We stop at a label.
We stop at an idea.
The problem with that is it leads to really rigid ways of thinking, rigid views about who and what we are and what's happening around us.
There's a great line in the Metta Sutta.
You know this line?
The wise are going to be better off by not having fixed views.
So this is a great thing to think about, our fixed views.
Can we be wiser about that?
But the idea is not just that you should be more broad-minded or more curious, which is a good thing.
There's a more fundamental question here: to notice the way you create views and hold onto views.
These thought exercises, like Zisheng's wheel with the hub removed, sound silly in a way, but actually they're digging into some deep waters.
Some things we do so automatically we don't see them.
So we need these strange devices of weird stories and taking hubs out of wheels.
If it can't really spin anymore, is it a wheel?
And it's interesting to just notice, with everything we conceptualize, how does it work for us?
What's the exact moment where it goes from being a wheel to a collection of wheel parts?
When's the exact moment that you take away enough parts that you can't even tell they're wheel parts?
They're just parts, just things, just something we see.
And at some point does the something drop away too, and we're just seeing shape and color?
No need to add a concept.
And at what point does the idea of shape and color, which is also an idea that we map onto reality, if there is such a thing, when does that drop away?
There's just some sense of a seer who's seeing, a seer who's experiencing, an experiencer who's noticing something.
And at what point does even that feeling, the feeling of being an experiencer, being a seer, drop away?
There's just the seeing, just this moment.
Meditation practice is wonderful because it can help us to recognize this vast array of things that's happening every moment.
Then we can go about it differently.
We can feel it and see it and understand it differently.
And that may really help us and help our world.

So the idea with teachings or wisdom is not just to get a better idea, but to understand something of the nature of making ideas and the ways that they're right and the ways that they're wrong inherently.
Never right and never quite wrong.
So you might think that the point of zazen, or meditation, is something about following the breath, probably Scott said in the library.
Something like that.
Did you say something like that?
Follow the breath?
And if you get lost in your thoughts, come back to the breath, right?
Sounds like a little project.
It might calm you down.
That would be good.
Feel a little better.
That would be nice.
It might help your immune system or something.
Calmer.
You might think it's all a project to get good at letting go of your thinking and just breathing.
But maybe one day, if you do this right, thinking will just stop bothering you so much and you can just breathe.
Maybe somebody will be really impressed by you if you could do that or something.
Well, that can happen.
The thinking can stop.
There's a lot of it, but it pauses from time to time.
Sometimes the thinking pauses and you don't even notice the thinking is paused, because who's the one doing the noticing?
The thinker, right?
So how's that person going to notice?
But actually, getting good at thinking or not thinking or breathing or not breathing is not the point of zazen.
The point of zazen is something more to do with developing a feeling, an appreciation, a sense, an understanding of just the flow of all of this.
Thoughts are thoughts.
Concepts are concepts.
Flowing and coalescing and changing moment to moment to moment.
Sometimes we believe them.
Sometimes we see through them in a certain way.
Sometimes we're brilliant.
Sometimes we're confused.
But really it's just the coming together of so many things moment by moment.
We're involved, but we are far from in charge, if you notice that.
So the classic way of speaking about emptiness is that all dharmas, meaning all things, are empty of something.
You can't have emptiness without empty of something.
The idea is that we don't realize what we're doing.
What we're doing is pouring something into everything we receive.

We perceive it and instantly and automatically pour this magical kind of goo in there, which leads the thing we're perceiving to seem separate and solid and to have a sort of quality to it, a sort of is-ness to it.
So we pour this stuff, this "I'm making this real through my perception" stuff, into our conceptions, and it appears to be a certain way.
The Buddhist sages had a word for the stuff that we pour into our conceptions.
That's interesting too to think about, what we have words for.
We don't have words for this stuff because we don't know it very well.
Anyway, they had a word for this process.
The thing that we pour in is called self-nature.
Svabhava in Sanskrit.
It's a sort of belief or understanding that things are separate, things are stable, things are permanent, at least for a while.
I mean, we all believe in impermanence, right?
None of us here believes completely in permanence, right?
That would be stupid.
But our way of believing in impermanence is not really impermanence, actually, is it?
It's like temporary permanence.
We would like a car to be permanent for at least about 12 years, right?
And then it can stop working.
That would be okay, right?
But we want permanence till then.
And we want permanence for ourselves.
Eighty years maybe, as long as our health is good.
We'd like that.
A little more than 80 is okay, too.
Is Edie still here?
I didn't mean to cut her off.
Shoot.
Take it back.
But of course we don't know.
So it's beautiful to get to bow at the altar up here, I hope.
And you can come bow at the altar yourself, too.
Not in the middle of formal practice, but when you're here, before or after or on your own.
You should definitely come bow at the altar.
What's wonderful right now is when you bow at the altar, there's a picture of Nancy there.
Especially if you knew Nancy.
Even if you didn't, it's beautiful to bow with an image of somebody on the altar.
So when somebody dies, it's so clear, right?
Our incredible resistance to impermanence can do nothing but melt away.
And it's difficult for us.
Because we've been pouring this self-nature into everything, trying to make things stick around, make things be what we think they are.
These teachings are not saying it isn't what you think it is, exactly.
There is someone named Nancy.
There is a lectern.
There is a car that we hope will start when we go back to our car.
So it's not that these things aren't.
These teachings suggest that we just get a lot more curious, though.
X really is X and Y really is Y, or is it?
Maybe X just appears to be X.
It's not that it's not X, but it's not really X in the way that we think it is.
Or maybe it's only X.
Its X-ness is a manifestation of coming together, a coalescence that's just there for an instant, and then something else happens.
So it's not X and it's not not X.
You have to talk like that when you're trying to talk about this stuff.
Maybe it's better not to talk about it.
The point being, if we pay attention, we start to see.
It takes some time.
Things are more fluid and dynamic, and not what we thought they were, than we can ever quite imagine.
This can sometimes be surprising and frightening, but it can also be wonderful.
It can also be liberating.
Because we too are that way, you can set down this burden of having to be yourself all the time.
That's our biggest job in the world, right?
It's hard work every day.
I've got to be myself.
I've got to keep this together.
Once the others find out I'm no good, I've got to keep it up.
So it's hard work, and that's the liberative quality of emptiness: we can soften, because I'm not this self exactly anyway.
There's some strange coming together in this moment.
We had some pictures out because we were looking through old pictures, looking for what pictures we had of Nancy for the memorial.
Seeing pictures of myself at 22, and then the next album over had a picture of me at 10 years old.
Is that the same person?
I put the same label on it.
I say, Tim, look, there's Tim.
It doesn't look the same.
It doesn't feel the same.
Of course, it's just an image on a picture now.
Did that person ever exist?
So it's true of everything, with everything we see and hear or feel.
Like the other day at the annual meeting, I showed some pictures of when we were building out this room.
When we first got here it was just an empty shell, a mix of plywood and concrete floor.
The concrete was about a half inch too high.
That was a problem.
And no lights, no heat, nothing.
It was just a shell, and we audaciously, because we were 20-somethings then, just said, we can deal with this.
We know what to do.
Maybe we were in our 30s by then, or the other pictures were in our 20s.
But anyway, those of us who were here then look at this room and we see it differently.
I can't help but see Jeff McKenna laying floor over there, and Bob laying out that wall and talking to me about his plans.
Bob and Lou Hinkley had kind of ridiculous repartee back and forth for hours and hours and hours.
So everything is colored by everything.
I'm not seeing the same room that anyone else is seeing.
We have this idea of an objective reality.
We think it's the same room, but it's not the same room.
And just for having seen those pictures, if you were there Saturday last, maybe you see this room a little differently too, but in a different way than I see it.
And if you're just hearing this from me now and you're wondering, wait, am I seeing it the right way?
There's no right way.
So is there exactly a room here?
It's just our view.
It's just our image.
It's just our conception.
This is all a little abstract, and I'm trying to be amusing about it.
So we'll keep listening.
I have to protect myself as somebody who's teaching something.
But I really want to encourage us to think about these things and notice about these things, not just think about them.
Am I holding a view here?
Am I mapping something onto something or someone, including myself?
Am I, through a fixed habitual conception, trying to make myself into something?
And how does that feel?
Often it feels bad.
It creates suffering, to try to impose our view on others and on ourselves.
It doesn't give us room to function.
It doesn't give us room to be totally and fully alive.
It doesn't give us space.

Isn't it funny to think that the way the hub works is the space in the middle?
It's the space in the middle that allows the hub to work.
It's that way for us too.
It's the space in us that allows us to function.
And we're so busily pouring this sticky Svabhava goop into ourselves and everything that there's no space left.
And it's painful.
Somehow we can function really at top performance nonetheless, but it's a painful kind of functioning, even if we're not aware of the pain.

That's chapter 11 according to Red Pine's translation.
There are apparently like 500 or something of those translations of the Dao Te Ching.
In his introduction, Red Pine said his Chinese teacher told him, once you feel a need to translate the Dao Te Ching, you're done.
That's time to retire.
They talk about it like that.
It seems like a good translation, and he didn't retire, so that's good.
So, chapter 11:
*Thirty spokes converge on a hub, but it's the emptiness that makes the wheel work.
Pots are fashioned from clay, but it's the hollow that makes the pot work.
Windows and doors are carved for a house, but it's the spaces that make the house work.
Existence makes something useful, but non-existence makes it work.*
Isn't that beautiful?
*Thirty spokes converge in a hub, but it's the emptiness that makes the wheel work.
Pots are fashioned from clay, but it's the hollow that makes the pot work.
Windows and doors are carved for a house, but it's the spaces that make the house work.
Existence makes something useful, but non-existence makes it work.*
And it's the same with life and death too, isn't it?

I said a little snippet the other day about the history of Nancy and the Sangha: part of what ended up making it work was the last years, when she actually wasn't here with her body, but she was making space.
She was helping to make it work.

Of course I'd love for you all to be here, but when you're not here, you're helping to make it work.
That's how it works to be a Xiu-Sou, by the way.
Carol's here visiting from Berkeley, about to be a Xiu-Sou.
Scott was just Xiu-Sou.

What have I done?
You think to yourself, gosh, I'm the hub, it all hangs off me now, and I'm going to be so central, and under the bright lights, and everyone's going to be paying attention to me.
Oh no, I can't do that.
You can think about another version of this in your life, where you have to be the central piece: horrifying.
But then you realize the hub doesn't make the wheel turn around.
The wheel turns itself around.
You just have to have the space in the middle.
You just have to have the space in the middle.
You just have to allow.
You just have to let the connections happen, let the spokes hook into you.
Maybe like Jeff McKenna at the Sundance.
I mean, that's not a good analogy.
That's a little more intense than being Xiu-Sou, I think.
But anyway, we don't have to make it all happen.
How could we make it all happen anyway?
What a silly myth we put in our heads.
That's one of those rigid, Svabhava-filled ideas, that I have to make it happen.
I can't make it happen.
We can only make it happen together.
That's the only way.
So it's good to remember that non-existence is important.
Our basic stance is the stance of existence, so of course non-existence is disturbing, sometimes frightening, horrifying.
We don't like people to be gone.
And it's beautiful in its way.
It's because we love each other.
We don't want us to be gone.
But when we're gone, we're not here to push the wheel around, maybe.
But when we're gone, we're still the space in the hub.
We're still allowing the Dharma wheel, the life wheel, the wheel that's bigger than any of our ideas, any of our conceptions.
We're allowing that to turn.
And we can only do that together, and we can only do that out of love.
That love is present even when we're pissed off at each other, or confused, or tired, or don't want it to be the way it is.
It's still there, because that's the quality of the space.
Emptiness sounds kind of cold when you hear about it.
They had to pick an English word for this concept, and emptiness sounds cold, but actually not at all.
So for once in my career, I ended before the end.
Does anyone have any thoughts or anything they'd like to voice?
Any empty words?
The good thing about emptiness, too, is it's freedom from performance anxiety, because you can't say it right.
Since you can't say it right, you can't say it wrong.
So you can just say it.
What do you say to emptiness?
Yay!
I think we're going to read a Thich Nhat Hanh book in the Heart Sutra class, and I think he has a little line like that in there.
Hurrah for emptiness!
But really, the hurrah also has to be a hurrah with tears, too, right? [unclear: "Mine's quiet words are the best."] Thank you for those, too.
